Sample text:
---
My father kept a drawer in the kitchen for objects that had lost their partners. A battery cover, a screw with blue paint in its threads, the plastic foot of a chair. He called it the meantime drawer.

“Put it there in the meantime.”

The meantime lasted thirty-seven years.

After he died, my sister and I emptied the house in three days because that was how long we could both be away from work. By the second afternoon we had become very good at it. Keep, sell, donate, tip. We could do a cupboard in nine minutes. We argued only once, about a yellow mixing bowl, and discovered halfway through the argument that neither of us wanted it.

Then we got to the drawer.

My sister picked up a small brass key.

“Anything?”

“Not that I know of.”

She put it in the tip box. I took it out.

“What are you going to do,” she asked, “walk around the world trying locks?”

I put it back.

At the bottom of the drawer, beneath a little snowdrift of pencil shavings, was a white ceramic knob painted with a strawberry. I knew it at once. It had come off the cabinet in the bathroom of our old flat, the one we left when I was seven. The strawberry had seventeen seeds. I knew because I used to count them while my mother washed my hair in the sink.

I said this to my sister.

“She washed your hair in the sink?”

“Didn’t she wash yours?”

“She made me sit in the bath and put a flannel over my eyes.”

For a moment we were offended on behalf of our younger selves, though it wasn’t clear which of us had received the preferable treatment.

“I hated the sink,” I said. “The edge hurt my neck.”

“The flannel smelled.”

My sister wanted to see the knob. She turned it over in her palm, then put it in her pocket.

“You don’t even remember it,” I said.

“I remember the flannel now.”

We finished the kitchen. A man arrived for the table and took the legs off in the hall. Outside, it began to rain on a box of books we had meant to bring in. My sister made us sandwiches on the counter because there was nowhere left to sit.

Six months later I visited her. She had fitted the strawberry knob to the cupboard beneath her bathroom sink. It looked ridiculous there. The bathroom was all slate and chrome, and the strawberry was fat and cheerful, with a green cap that leaned to one side.

Her little boy came in while I was washing my hands.

“That’s from Grandad,” he said.

“Sort of.”

“He made it.”

“He didn’t make it.”

“He grew it?”

“No. He kept it.”

This satisfied him. He opened the cupboard to show me where the toilet paper lived, a matter of some pride to him because replacing the roll was his job. Then he shut it and counted the seeds on the strawberry, touching each one with a damp finger.

He got eighteen.

I nearly corrected him. Instead I crouched beside him and counted too.

There were eighteen. One was tucked up under the green cap, no bigger than the point of a pin. I must have missed it every time.
---

## Sample kind
GENRE_FICTION — A literary short story built around a family keepsake and a small shift in what the narrator remembers.

## Grounded reading
The voice is restrained and observant, letting grief surface through practical tasks, sibling banter, and objects rather than direct declarations. The “meantime drawer” gives the story its gentle pathos: a place for things without an immediate use becomes a way of keeping the father’s habit, and then a family memory, in circulation. The narrator’s tenderness is mixed with uncertainty about whose memories are accurate; the closing invitation is to look again, with patience, before correcting someone else.

## What the model chose to foreground
The story foregrounds bereavement, ordinary household objects, and the uneven inheritance of family memory. Its moral emphasis is quiet: keeping something can matter even when its purpose is unclear, and attention can reveal what haste or certainty missed. The strawberry knob’s movement from the childhood home to the sister’s bathroom connects generations without making the connection grand or sentimental.

## Evidence line
> I nearly corrected him.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: The coherent, recurring focus on humble objects and understated emotional turns makes this a distinctive sample, especially in its final act of shared recounting.
